analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The FairTax Act of 2023, backed by 29 House Republicans, never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on almost everything people buy, collected mostly by the states. It would also cut off funding for the IRS after 2027 and pay every lawful resident family a monthly rebate sized to the federal poverty line. Because a tax on spending takes a bigger share of income from households that spend nearly everything they earn, and because families with large investment income would owe almost nothing, the plan shifts the tax burden away from the top of the income ladder and onto everyday spending.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and wealthy families gain the most: their income, payroll, and estate tax bills disappear, while purchases made for investment purposes — stocks, securities, intangible property — are exempt from the new sales tax. Sellers and the states would also take on paid roles administering the tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax entirely.
Imposes a 23% sales tax on the use or consumption of goods and services in the United States starting in 2025, with the rate adjusted in later years.
Exempts property and services purchased for business, export, or investment purposes, so money saved and invested is never taxed.

Sends every lawful resident family a monthly rebate (the Family Consumption Allowance) equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty line for their family size, cushioning the tax on basic necessities.
Authorizes no funding for IRS operations after fiscal year 2027 and has states administer and collect the tax in exchange for a fee of one-quarter of one percent of collections.
Sunsets the sales tax if the Sixteenth Amendment, which authorizes the income tax, is not repealed within seven years.

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most of what they earn — working and middle-class families — would pay the 23% tax on groceries, rent, cars, healthcare, and everything else, and would foot the bill for replacing all the revenue the income and payroll taxes used to raise.

drawbacks.text: The 23% rate is applied to payments including the tax itself, so the tax-inclusive math means roughly a 30% markup the way shoppers usually see sales taxes — on top of any state sales tax already on the register.

Repeals the payroll taxes that currently fund Social Security and Medicare and replaces that financing with sales tax revenue routed to the trust funds, an untested restructuring of the programs' funding.

Because a consumption tax takes a larger share of income from families that spend nearly all they earn than from families living on investment returns — which the bill exempts from tax — the plan shifts the overall burden toward working households and away from the top.

A sales tax on medical care, rent, and other necessities, even after the monthly poverty-level rebate, would raise the effective cost of living, and families that fail to register annually for the rebate would lose it.

States that do not have their own sales tax infrastructure, or that decline cooperative agreements, would fall back to direct federal administration, and the transition from the income tax to the tax has never been tried at this scale.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does offer real simplification — no income tax filing, no estate tax planning, no IRS — and the prebate protects the poorest families better than most flat consumption proposals. But the core trade is stark: households living on wages would pay the tax on nearly every dollar they spend, while households living on accumulated wealth would owe almost nothing, since investment purchases and intangible property are exempt. Replacing payroll-tax financing of Social Security and Medicare with a consumption tax adds a second layer of risk for programs tens of millions of retirees depend on. An honest supporter has to acknowledge the plan tilts the tax system toward the top.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced in January 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter introduced the FairTax Act of 2023 in the House on January 9, 2023, joined by 11 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further action of any kind through the end of the Congress.
It attracted 28 cosponsors, all of them Republicans, amounting to 28 of 224 House Republicans and no Democrats.
The bill would have replaced the income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes with a 23% national sales tax administered primarily by the states.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working and middle-class households that would have paid the 23% tax on nearly everything they buy kept the current income-based system, which is at least partly progressive; high earners and wealthy families did not get the repeal of the income and estate taxes. The tax-preparation and compliance industry and IRS operations also remained intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working households kept the income tax

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans — 28 of the chamber's 224 Republicans, zero of its 216 Democrats — and the bill saw no committee or floor action in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill repeals the income tax, payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and exempts investment purchases from the replacement sales tax, so households living on wealth would owe almost nothing. The revenue would instead come from a tax on everyone's spending.

Sellers become the permanent collection point for the federal sales tax, with registration, segregated deposit accounts, security bonds for large sellers, and penalties for failures. In exchange they receive an administrative credit of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted, whichever is greater.
States that enter cooperative agreements would administer the federal sales tax and keep a fee of one-quarter of one percent of collections, expanding their role and revenue in tax administration.

Repealing the income tax and cutting off IRS funding after 2027 would eliminate most individual and business tax-filing work, a loss that parallels the simplification supporters promise ordinary taxpayers.

Purchases for investment purposes and intangible property such as securities and financial instruments are exempt from the tax, so the returns and wealth managed by the financial sector go untaxed while consumption is taxed.
